passages.t: Teachers, and the small things that steer
passages.happening:
“Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly. We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body” (verses 1-2).

Then three pictures. “When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal. Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined” (verses 3-4).

“In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
James has already said, ‘slow to speak’ (1:19), and warned against an unbridled tongue (1:26). Now he starts with the people whose work is speaking: teachers.

In the early church teachers were honoured. They are named among God's gifts to the church, and in the synagogue a teacher of the law was respected. So the role attracted people who wanted the honour for its own sake. Jesus himself warned his disciples not to seek the title ‘Rabbi’. James says: not many of you should rush into it, because teachers will answer to God for what they taught.

And he includes himself. ‘We who teach.’ ‘We all stumble.’ James does not speak as someone who has mastered his tongue. He stands inside the warning.

‘Perfect’ here means mature, whole. If anyone could fully control his speech, he could control everything else too. No one does.

Then the pictures, each from daily life. A small metal bit, joined to the reins, turns a strong horse. A small steering oar at the back of a great merchant ship, held by one pilot, sets its course against the wind. Small things steer large ones. So does the tongue: a few words can set the direction of a life, a family or a church.

And small things can destroy large ones. In the dry summers of the land, brush and forest fires were a constant danger. One spark could burn a hillside.
passages.ot:
Israel's priests were teachers, and the prophet Malachi set out their high calling: “For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts” (Malachi 2:7).

God told Ezekiel that a watchman who failed to warn would answer for it: “I will hold you responsible for his blood” (Ezekiel 3:18).

And Proverbs is full of the power of small words: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit” (Proverbs 18:21). And, “Like charcoal for embers and wood for fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife” (Proverbs 26:21).
passages.hard:
‘We who teach will be judged more strictly.’ Should this frighten everyone who teaches a Sunday class or leads a Bible study?

It should make teachers careful, not afraid. James is not telling believers to stop teaching; the church needs teachers, and the New Testament counts them a gift. He is warning against seeking the role for status, and reminding every teacher that words spoken in God's name carry weight. The same letter says that God gives wisdom ‘generously to all without finding fault’ to anyone who asks (1:5).

The warning also cuts the other way. Teachers and leaders are accountable. Their position does not put them above correction. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: If you teach in any way, at church, at home or at work, ask whether you want the role or the honour. Ask whether you stand inside your own teaching. And ask what small words of yours this week have steered someone, for good or ill.

passages.t: A fire, and a spring that cannot give two waters
passages.happening:
“The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell” (verse 6).

“All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man, but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (verses 7-8).

“With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness. Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be! Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water” (verses 9-12).
passages.hearers:
James's language grows stronger. The tongue is not only a spark; it is a fire. It is ‘a world of wickedness’, a whole world of evil packed into one small part of the body. It ‘pollutes the whole person’ and sets ‘the course of his life’ on fire.

‘Hell’ here translates Gehenna. The name comes from the Valley of Hinnom, on the south side of Jerusalem. In the days of the kings of Judah, children were sacrificed by fire there to foreign gods. In later Jewish thought, the valley became a name for the place of final judgment. Outside the Gospels, where Jesus uses the word several times, this is the only place in the New Testament it appears. James means that destructive speech draws its fire from evil itself.

People can tame lions, birds, snakes and sea creatures. But no one can tame the tongue. James is not saying the tongue has a life of its own. It speaks what is in the heart. Jesus said, ‘out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks’.

Then the deepest point. With one tongue we praise God, and with the same tongue we curse people. But people are made in God's likeness. To curse a person is to dishonour the God whose image that person bears. You cannot honestly bless the King and spit on his portrait.

The last pictures come from the land. A spring gives either fresh water or salt water, not both; in a dry country, a salty spring was useless. A fig tree does not grow olives. Fig, olive and grape were the three great crops of the land, and every hearer knew that each tree bears its own fruit. A mouth that both blesses and curses shows a heart divided.
passages.ot:
James's reason for not cursing people comes from the first page of the Bible: “Then God said, ‘Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness’” (Genesis 1:26). After the flood, God gave the same reason for protecting human life: “for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6).

The Valley of Hinnom is named in the account of King Josiah's reform: “He also desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech” (2 Kings 23:10).

The psalms often picture cruel words as poison: “They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips” (Psalm 140:3). And they pray for help: “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips” (Psalm 141:3).
passages.hard:
‘No man can tame the tongue.’ If no one can, why does James tell us to try?

James is honest. No one masters speech by willpower. Everyone stumbles. But that is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to look beyond ourselves. The tongue speaks from the heart, so the cure begins with the heart, and that is God's work. In this same letter James promises that God gives wisdom to anyone who asks (1:5), and in the next verses he describes the wisdom from above, which is ‘peace-loving’ and ‘full of mercy’. What no person can tame, God can change.

James does not treat cruel words lightly, and neither should anyone who has been on the receiving end of them. Words can do real harm. If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Think back over your words in the last day. Ask where your tongue blessed God and then cursed, mocked or belittled someone made in his image. Ask what your words show about your heart. And ask God for the change that willpower alone cannot bring.

passages.happening:
“Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom. But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth” (verses 13-14).

“Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice” (verses 15-16).

“But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness” (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
James returns to wisdom, which he first raised in 1:5. And he ties it to everything he has just said about the tongue. The tongue shows whether a person's wisdom comes from above or from below.

‘Who is wise?’ In a church where people competed to teach, many would have liked to answer, ‘I am.’ James says: then show it, not by clever talk, but by a good life and by deeds done humbly.

Then he describes a counterfeit wisdom. It can be clever and persuasive. But underneath are ‘bitter jealousy and selfish ambition’. ‘Selfish ambition’ means self-seeking, rivalry. That kind of wisdom is ‘earthly’, bounded by this world; ‘unspiritual’, belonging to the natural self rather than to God's Spirit; and ‘demonic’, like the demons in its spirit. Its fruit is ‘disorder’: quarrels, factions, a church pulled apart. Chapter 4 opens with exactly that.

Then the true wisdom, described like a portrait. First ‘pure’, without mixed motives. Then ‘peace-loving’, ‘gentle’, ‘accommodating’ (ready to listen and yield), ‘full of mercy and good fruit’, ‘impartial’ (it does not play favourites, as in chapter 2), and ‘sincere’ (without a mask). It reads like a picture of Jesus himself.

The last line is a small proverb. People who make peace, and sow it peacefully, will harvest a right life. Jesus said, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers.’
passages.ot:
The wisdom books describe wisdom by its fruit: “All her ways are pleasant, and all her paths are peaceful” (Proverbs 3:17). And they tie wisdom to humility: “When pride comes, disgrace follows, but with humility comes wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2).

Isaiah promises that righteousness will bear the fruit of peace: “The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever” (Isaiah 32:17).

And Proverbs prizes the person who rules himself: “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city” (Proverbs 16:32).
passages.hard:
‘Earthly, unspiritual, demonic.’ Is James saying that jealous or ambitious people are possessed by demons? And is all ambition wrong?

No to both. The word translated ‘demonic’ means ‘demon-like’. James is describing what this false wisdom is like and where its spirit comes from. He is not diagnosing a person, and he gives no one licence to call a fellow believer possessed because they disagree. He names jealousy and self-seeking, things found in every heart, his own included, as he has already said: ‘We all stumble’.

And the word for ‘selfish ambition’ means rivalry and self-seeking, working for yourself at the cost of others. James is not condemning every wish to do good work well. He is condemning the drive to get ahead by pushing others down, which tears a church apart.

So the answer is not to hunt for the demon in someone else. It is to look honestly at our own hearts, to confess what we find there, and to ask God for the wisdom that is ‘first of all pure, then peace-loving’.
passages.asks: Ask how your wisdom shows: in what you say, or in how you live. Ask whether jealousy or ambition is at work in you, even under good words. Read the list in verse 17 slowly and ask which of those you most lack. Then ask God for it, as James promised you may.
